title: Pressure of record dates
summary: One missed note could end your call.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Well that was -- I meant best in that sense, yes. Best trained, I should say. A great deal depended on your ability to read because you would -- on a record date you would come in and they would take it down once, down to see if the arranger or copyist had put some wrong notes in it, then they'd do it two or three times for the people in the booth to balance with the singer, and then you'd record it. And before tape came in, you had to record it perfectly because there was no splicing tape, you know. And God help you if you missed a note. There was a saying, no matter how good your reputation was, you were only as good as your last note. If you cracked that last note, you weren't called again.

Because there were people around -- I remember this trumpet player I used to work with, left for Florida. And when the clock got to the last two or three minutes, he would start missing notes so we'd go into overtime. I remember Mitch Miller caught onto that. "You're through. You don't ever work here again." Because he knew Red and --
That was quite an era then, those great musicians.
